dtc_codes.title_en: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor
dtc_codes.description_en: Code C0031 (Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor) sets when the ABS module loses a valid electrical signal from a wheel speed sensor -- the circuit reads open, shorted low or high, drops out intermittently, fails to correlate with the other three wheels, or reports an incorrect component installed. The diagnosis and repair are identical at every corner: a corroded or unplugged connector, a chafed harness conductor rubbing on the strut or subframe, or a failed Hall-effect/variable-reluctance sensor element. This is distinct from a tone-ring or mechanical fault, where the wiring and sensor test fine but the signal is noisy or absent because of physical damage at the reluctor wheel.

dtc_codes.title_en: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor Supply
dtc_codes.description_en: Code C0035 (Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor Supply) sets when the ABS module loses a valid electrical signal from a wheel speed sensor -- the circuit reads open, shorted low or high, drops out intermittently, fails to correlate with the other three wheels, or reports an incorrect component installed. The diagnosis and repair are identical at every corner: a corroded or unplugged connector, a chafed harness conductor rubbing on the strut or subframe, or a failed Hall-effect/variable-reluctance sensor element. This is distinct from a tone-ring or mechanical fault, where the wiring and sensor test fine but the signal is noisy or absent because of physical damage at the reluctor wheel.

dtc_codes.title_en: Brake Pedal Switch A
dtc_codes.description_en: Code C0040 (Brake Pedal Switch A) sets when the module sees an implausible state from the brake pedal switch(es) that both illuminate the stop lamps and tell the ABS/cruise/shift-interlock systems the brake pedal is applied -- the switch stays closed, stays open, or the two redundant switch channels disagree with each other. A misadjusted switch plunger, a worn switch contact, or corrosion at the switch connector near the pedal bracket are the common causes. Because this switch also feeds the stop lamps and brake-transmission shift interlock, a fault here can cause symptoms well beyond ABS, from stuck-on brake lights to a shifter that will not release from Park.

dtc_codes.title_en: A Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0011 (A Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance Bank 1) sets when a camshaft phaser reaches a timing position beyond commanded limits or becomes stuck rather than responding to duty-cycle commands. Root causes are sludge or low oil pressure starving the phaser, a worn phaser with excessive internal slack, a stuck oil control valve, or a mis-timed chain/belt from prior service.

dtc_codes.title_en: Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation Bank 1 Sensor A
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0016 (Crankshaft Position - Camshaft Position Correlation Bank 1 Sensor A) sets when the ECM compares crankshaft and camshaft position signals and finds their relative timing outside the expected window, or cannot establish a stable engine position sync. This is most often caused by timing chain/belt stretch or a jumped tooth, a failing crankshaft or camshaft position sensor, worn tensioner/guides, or reluctor-wheel damage.

dtc_codes.title_en: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0101 (Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance) sets when the ECM detects an implausible signal from the mass air flow sensor — reported airflow disagrees with throttle position and engine speed, or the signal voltage leaves its calibrated window. The most common physical causes are a contaminated MAF sensing element, unmetered air entering the intake downstream of the sensor, and chafed or corroded wiring in the sensor's 5V reference / signal-return circuit.

dtc_codes.title_en: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0102 (Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low) sets when the ECM detects an implausible signal from the mass air flow sensor — reported airflow disagrees with throttle position and engine speed, or the signal voltage leaves its calibrated window. The most common physical causes are a contaminated MAF sensing element, unmetered air entering the intake downstream of the sensor, and chafed or corroded wiring in the sensor's 5V reference / signal-return circuit.

dtc_codes.title_en: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0106 (Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance) sets when the ECM sees an open, shorted, or implausible voltage from the MAP/barometric pressure sensor circuit, or the reading is simply too low for the current altitude. Causes are a cracked or oil-fouled vacuum port, a failed sensor element, or damaged sensor wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0113 (Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1) sets when the ECM sees an open, shorted, or implausible resistance from an intake air temperature sensor (any position/bank), or a correlation mismatch against a related ambient or fuel temperature signal. Causes are a corroded connector, a failed thermistor element, or chafed harness wiring near the intake tract.

dtc_codes.title_en: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0114 (Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent Bank 1) sets when the ECM sees an open, shorted, or implausible resistance from an intake air temperature sensor (any position/bank), or a correlation mismatch against a related ambient or fuel temperature signal. Causes are a corroded connector, a failed thermistor element, or chafed harness wiring near the intake tract.

dtc_codes.title_en: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0118 (Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High) sets when the ECM sees an open, shorted, or implausible resistance from an engine or radiator coolant temperature sensor, or a correlation mismatch between redundant coolant/oil/ambient temperature signals. Causes are a corroded connector, a failed thermistor element, low coolant exposing the sensor tip, or chafed wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0121 (Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-range voltage, or an implausible rate of change, from a throttle body or accelerator pedal position sensor channel. Causes are a worn sensor track, a corroded connector, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0128 (Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)) sets when engine coolant fails to reach or maintain its regulating temperature within the expected time, or coolant flow/circulation is judged insufficient. Causes are a thermostat stuck open, a low coolant level, a failing water pump, or a chronically cold operating condition combined with a stuck-open thermostat.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0131 (O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, a stuck/biased voltage, or no signal activity from an oxygen sensor's signal circuit. Causes are a contaminated or worn-out sensor element, an exhaust leak near the sensor bung skewing readings, or damaged sensor wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0133 (O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1) sets when an oxygen sensor takes longer than the calibrated time to transition between rich and lean voltage states. This is typically a sensor element that has aged or been contaminated by silicone, oil ash, or coolant, though an exhaust leak that dilutes the sample can also slow the switching response.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0135 (O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-spec resistance in the internal heater element of an oxygen sensor, or the heater fails to bring the sensor to operating temperature within the expected time. This is almost always a degraded heater element inside the O2 sensor itself, though a blown fuse, relay, or chafed heater wiring can also be responsible.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0138 (O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, a stuck/biased voltage, or no signal activity from an oxygen sensor's signal circuit. Causes are a contaminated or worn-out sensor element, an exhaust leak near the sensor bung skewing readings, or damaged sensor wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0141 (O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-spec resistance in the internal heater element of an oxygen sensor, or the heater fails to bring the sensor to operating temperature within the expected time. This is almost always a degraded heater element inside the O2 sensor itself, though a blown fuse, relay, or chafed heater wiring can also be responsible.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Too Lean Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0171 (System Too Lean Bank 1) sets when the ECM must add more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a lean condition on the indicated bank. The leading causes are a vacuum or intake air leak downstream of the MAF, a weak fuel pump or clogged filter, or a leaking exhaust manifold gasket confusing the upstream O2 sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Too Rich Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0172 (System Too Rich Bank 1) sets when the ECM must remove more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a rich condition on the indicated bank. Leading causes are a leaking fuel injector, a stuck-open fuel pressure regulator, a fouled MAF sensor overreporting airflow, or a failing fuel pressure sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Too Lean Bank 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0174 (System Too Lean Bank 2) sets when the ECM must add more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a lean condition on the indicated bank. The leading causes are a vacuum or intake air leak downstream of the MAF, a weak fuel pump or clogged filter, or a leaking exhaust manifold gasket confusing the upstream O2 sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Too Rich Bank 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0175 (System Too Rich Bank 2) sets when the ECM must remove more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a rich condition on the indicated bank. Leading causes are a leaking fuel injector, a stuck-open fuel pressure regulator, a fouled MAF sensor overreporting airflow, or a failing fuel pressure sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
dtc_codes.title_vi: Phát hiện bỏ máy ngẫu nhiên / nhiều xi-lanh
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0300 (Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected) sets when the ECM's crankshaft-acceleration misfire monitor counts combustion events across multiple cylinders (or an undifferentiated pattern) beyond the calibrated threshold, including variants triggered by a low fuel level, a cold-start window, or a commanded fuel cutoff. Because no single cylinder is isolated, the cause is almost always something that affects the whole engine at once: a vacuum leak, worn spark plugs across the set, a weak fuel pump/low fuel level, or a base ignition timing/reluctor fault.
dtc_codes.description_vi: ECU phát hiện hiện tượng bỏ máy xảy ra ngẫu nhiên hoặc trên nhiều xi-lanh.

dtc_codes.title_en: Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0301 (Cylinder 1 Misfire Detected) sets when the ECM's misfire monitor isolates repeated combustion events lost on one specific cylinder (or, for the unspecified variant, a single cylinder it cannot pin down). The diagnosis path is identical regardless of which cylinder number is reported: the fault lives in that cylinder's ignition, fuel delivery, or mechanical sealing, most commonly a fouled spark plug or failing coil, a clogged or leaking injector, or low compression from a burnt valve or worn rings.

The diagnosis path is identical regardless of which cylinder number is reported: the fault lives in that cylinder's ignition, fuel delivery, or mechanical sealing, most commonly a fouled spark plug or failing coil, a clogged or leaking injector, or low compression from a burnt valve or worn rings.

dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0306 (Cylinder 6 Misfire Detected) sets when the ECM's misfire monitor isolates repeated combustion events lost on one specific cylinder (or, for the unspecified variant, a single cylinder it cannot pin down). dtc_codes.title_en: Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor A Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0325 (Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor A Circuit) sets when the ECM detects an open circuit, out-of-range voltage, or a total loss of signal from a knock (combustion vibration) sensor used to retard timing and protect the engine from detonation, or when the overall knock control system itself reports an internal error. Physical causes are a failed piezoelectric sensor element, an improperly torqued sensor (knock sensors are torque-sensitive and read incorrectly if over- or under-tightened), or chafed/corroded wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0335 (Crankshaft Position Sensor A Circuit) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, out-of-range voltage, no signal, or an erratic pulse pattern from a crankshaft position sensor (or, on older distributor-based ignition systems, the distributor's engine-speed pickup that serves the same function). Common causes are a sensor with too large an air gap to the reluctor wheel, metal debris bridging the sensor tip, a corroded connector, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1 or Single Sensor
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0340 (Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1 or Single Sensor) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, out-of-range voltage, or an erratic signal from the primary camshaft position sensor used for cylinder identification and cam-to-crank correlation — distinct from a VVT phaser's own actuator-position feedback sensor. Common causes are a corroded connector, a worn or contaminated reluctor/trigger wheel on the camshaft, an incorrect air gap, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 or Single Sensor
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0341 (Camshaft Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 or Single Sensor) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, out-of-range voltage, or an erratic signal from the primary camshaft position sensor used for cylinder identification and cam-to-crank correlation — distinct from a VVT phaser's own actuator-position feedback sensor. Common causes are a corroded connector, a worn or contaminated reluctor/trigger wheel on the camshaft, an incorrect air gap, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0401 (EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected) sets when the ECM commands a specific EGR flow rate (valve A or valve B on dual-EGR platforms) and the measured intake or exhaust response indicates the actual flow is significantly less or more than commanded. Insufficient flow is most often a carbon-clogged EGR passage, valve, or cooler; excessive flow points to a valve stuck partially open or a failed position sensor causing the ECM to over-command it.

dtc_codes.title_en: EGR A Flow Excessive Detected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0402 (EGR A Flow Excessive Detected) sets when the ECM commands a specific EGR flow rate (valve A or valve B on dual-EGR platforms) and the measured intake or exhaust response indicates the actual flow is significantly less or more than commanded. Insufficient flow is most often a carbon-clogged EGR passage, valve, or cooler; excessive flow points to a valve stuck partially open or a failed position sensor causing the ECM to over-command it.

dtc_codes.title_en: EGR A Control Circuit/Open
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0403 (EGR A Control Circuit/Open) sets when the ECM detects an open circuit, out-of-range voltage, a learning-limit exceeded condition, or a mechanically stuck-open/stuck-closed report while driving an EGR control valve, an EGR throttle valve used to assist EGR flow, or the associated control processor. Causes are a failed EGR valve/throttle solenoid or motor, a corroded connector, carbon buildup mechanically jamming the valve, or damaged control wiring back to the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0411 (AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected) sets when the ECM commands the secondary air injection system (used to inject fresh air into the exhaust during cold start to speed catalyst light-off and reduce emissions) and detects incorrect flow, an open/shorted switching valve circuit, or a control circuit fault. Causes are a seized or failed AIR pump, a stuck or corroded switching/check valve, a collapsed or leaking air delivery hose, or damaged wiring to the pump/valve.

dtc_codes.title_en: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
dtc_codes.title_vi: Hiệu suất bộ xúc tác dưới ngưỡng — Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0420 (Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1) sets when the ECM compares pre- and post-catalyst oxygen sensor switching activity and finds the catalyst (or a specific catalyst brick on multi-brick systems) is no longer storing/releasing oxygen efficiently enough to meet emissions thresholds. The dominant cause is a catalyst that has aged out or been chemically poisoned (oil consumption, coolant leak into the exhaust, or leaded/high-sulfur fuel), though a persistent rich/lean fuel condition or an exhaust leak feeding false switching data can also trigger it.
dtc_codes.description_vi: Hiệu suất bộ xúc tác ở bank 1 thấp hơn ngưỡng giám sát của ECU.

dtc_codes.title_en: Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0430 (Catalyst System Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2) sets when the ECM compares pre- and post-catalyst oxygen sensor switching activity and finds the catalyst (or a specific catalyst brick on multi-brick systems) is no longer storing/releasing oxygen efficiently enough to meet emissions thresholds. The dominant cause is a catalyst that has aged out or been chemically poisoned (oil consumption, coolant leak into the exhaust, or leaded/high-sulfur fuel), though a persistent rich/lean fuel condition or an exhaust leak feeding false switching data can also trigger it.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0440 (EVAP System) sets when the EVAP leak-detection monitor cannot hold vacuum or pressure in the fuel vapor system within its small-leak threshold (typically a 0.020 in. equivalent orifice), including the tighter very-small-leak threshold and the fuel-tank-side/fresh-air-side variants used on natural-vacuum leak detection systems, or when the general EVAP system monitor itself fails. The dominant causes are a loose or worn fuel filler cap, a cracked EVAP hose, or a purge/vent solenoid that no longer seals.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Incorrect Purge Flow
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0441 (EVAP System Incorrect Purge Flow) sets when the ECM commands EVAP purge and the resulting flow through the purge line — measured by fuel trim shift, a purge flow sensor, or line pressure — is significantly higher or lower than expected for the commanded duty cycle, including the high-load purge line performance variant used on turbocharged/boosted platforms. Causes are a partially clogged purge line or canister restricting flow, a purge solenoid that leaks or does not open fully, or a collapsed/pinched purge hose under vacuum.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Leak Detected (small leak)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0442 (EVAP System Leak Detected (small leak)) sets when the EVAP leak-detection monitor cannot hold vacuum or pressure in the fuel vapor system within its small-leak threshold (typically a 0.020 in. equivalent orifice), including the tighter very-small-leak threshold and the fuel-tank-side/fresh-air-side variants used on natural-vacuum leak detection systems, or when the general EVAP system monitor itself fails. The dominant causes are a loose or worn fuel filler cap, a cracked EVAP hose, or a purge/vent solenoid that no longer seals.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Vent Control Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0446 (EVAP System Vent Control Circuit) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-range condition while driving the EVAP canister vent solenoid, the normally-open valve that must seal the system to atmosphere during a leak test. Causes are a failed solenoid coil, a corroded or unseated connector, debris/ice jamming the valve, or damaged wiring between the ECM and the solenoid.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Leak Detected - Large Leak
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0455 (EVAP System Leak Detected - Large Leak) sets when the EVAP leak-detection monitor detects a leak far larger than the small-leak threshold (roughly equivalent to a 0.040 in. orifice or bigger), including the fuel-tank-side and fresh-air-side variants on natural-vacuum leak detection systems. This points to a substantially open path to atmosphere: a fuel cap left off or badly damaged, a disconnected or split EVAP hose, or a canister/valve that has failed open.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Leak Detected (very small leak)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0456 (EVAP System Leak Detected (very small leak)) sets when the EVAP leak-detection monitor cannot hold vacuum or pressure in the fuel vapor system within its small-leak threshold (typically a 0.020 in. equivalent orifice), including the tighter very-small-leak threshold and the fuel-tank-side/fresh-air-side variants used on natural-vacuum leak detection systems, or when the general EVAP system monitor itself fails. The dominant causes are a loose or worn fuel filler cap, a cracked EVAP hose, or a purge/vent solenoid that no longer seals.

dtc_codes.title_en: EVAP System Leak Detected (fuel cap loose/off)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0457 (EVAP System Leak Detected (fuel cap loose/off)) sets when the EVAP leak-detection monitor cannot hold vacuum or pressure in the fuel vapor system within its small-leak threshold (typically a 0.020 in. equivalent orifice), including the tighter very-small-leak threshold and the fuel-tank-side/fresh-air-side variants used on natural-vacuum leak detection systems, or when the general EVAP system monitor itself fails. The dominant causes are a loose or worn fuel filler cap, a cracked EVAP hose, or a purge/vent solenoid that no longer seals.

dtc_codes.title_en: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0500 (Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit) sets when the ECM loses, or receives an implausible, vehicle speed signal from the primary VSS/output-shaft speed source used for speedometer, cruise control, ABS coordination, and shift scheduling. The signal is usually a toothed-wheel/magnetic or Hall-effect pickup, so the common causes are a damaged tone ring, an air-gap or debris problem at the sensor tip, a corroded connector, or chafed sensor wiring shorted to power/ground.

dtc_codes.title_en: Idle Control System
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0505 (Idle Control System) sets when commanded idle RPM (or, on diesel platforms, idle fuel quantity) does not match the ECM's target, or the idle air control actuator's circuit reports an open/out-of-range condition. Root causes are a carbon-fouled IAC valve or throttle bore restricting airflow, an unmetered vacuum/intake air leak that pushes idle high, a sticking throttle plate, or a failed IAC motor/solenoid and its wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Idle Control System RPM - Lower Than Expected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0506 (Idle Control System RPM - Lower Than Expected) sets when commanded idle RPM (or, on diesel platforms, idle fuel quantity) does not match the ECM's target, or the idle air control actuator's circuit reports an open/out-of-range condition. Root causes are a carbon-fouled IAC valve or throttle bore restricting airflow, an unmetered vacuum/intake air leak that pushes idle high, a sticking throttle plate, or a failed IAC motor/solenoid and its wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Idle Control System RPM - Higher Than Expected
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0507 (Idle Control System RPM - Higher Than Expected) sets when commanded idle RPM (or, on diesel platforms, idle fuel quantity) does not match the ECM's target, or the idle air control actuator's circuit reports an open/out-of-range condition. Root causes are a carbon-fouled IAC valve or throttle bore restricting airflow, an unmetered vacuum/intake air leak that pushes idle high, a sticking throttle plate, or a failed IAC motor/solenoid and its wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Voltage Low
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0562 (System Voltage Low) sets when the ECM's own B+ sense circuit measures system voltage outside its normal window or fluctuating erratically, pointing at the vehicle's overall charging/electrical system rather than a single sensor. Causes are a weak or failing battery, a charging system undercharging or overcharging, corroded main power/ground straps, or a parasitic draw combined with marginal alternator output.
dtc_codes.description_vi: Điện áp nguồn hệ thống thấp hơn dải vận hành mà ECU mong đợi.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Voltage High
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0563 (System Voltage High) sets when the ECM's own B+ sense circuit measures system voltage outside its normal window or fluctuating erratically, pointing at the vehicle's overall charging/electrical system rather than a single sensor. Causes are a weak or failing battery, a charging system undercharging or overcharging, corroded main power/ground straps, or a parasitic draw combined with marginal alternator output.

dtc_codes.title_en: Internal Control Module Memory Checksum Error
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0601 (Internal Control Module Memory Checksum Error) sets when a control module's (ECM, PCM, or TCM) internal self-test finds its memory (RAM/ROM/EEPROM/NVRAM/checksum), processor, or an internal signal-processing channel is not functioning correctly. Unlike a sensor circuit fault, this points at the module's own hardware, so the fix path is reflashing the module's software first and, if the fault returns, replacing the module rather than chasing external wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Control Module Processor
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0606 (Control Module Processor) sets when a control module's (ECM, PCM, or TCM) internal self-test finds its memory (RAM/ROM/EEPROM/NVRAM/checksum), processor, or an internal signal-processing channel is not functioning correctly. Unlike a sensor circuit fault, this points at the module's own hardware, so the fix path is reflashing the module's software first and, if the fault returns, replacing the module rather than chasing external wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Transmission Control System (MIL Request)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0700 (Transmission Control System (MIL Request)) sets when the TCM's overall self-check strategy — as opposed to any single sensor — requests the MIL, finds an electrical fault on its main harness, or judges its adaptive shift strategy is out of range. Causes are low or contaminated transmission fluid, a TCM software issue, an aftermarket electrical accessory disrupting the TCM's power/ground, or a wiring fault on the main TCM harness connector.

dtc_codes.title_en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input)
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0705 (Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input)) sets when the TCM sees an open, shorted, or implausible signal from the transmission range sensor that reports gear-selector position (Park/Reverse/Neutral/Drive/Low) to the ECM/TCM. Causes are a maladjusted or worn range sensor at the shift shaft, transmission fluid contamination fouling the sensor, or chafed wiring at the connector on the transmission case.

dtc_codes.title_en: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0706 (Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance) sets when the TCM sees an open, shorted, or implausible signal from the transmission range sensor that reports gear-selector position (Park/Reverse/Neutral/Drive/Low) to the ECM/TCM. Causes are a maladjusted or worn range sensor at the shift shaft, transmission fluid contamination fouling the sensor, or chafed wiring at the connector on the transmission case.

dtc_codes.title_en: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0715 (Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit) sets when the TCM loses, or receives an implausible, input/turbine shaft speed signal used for shift scheduling and torque converter clutch control. Causes are a damaged reluctor wheel, debris or metal shavings at the sensor tip, a corroded connector, or chafed wiring inside the transmission harness.

dtc_codes.title_en: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0720 (Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit) sets when the TCM loses, receives an implausible, or loses direction information from the transmission output shaft speed sensor used for shift scheduling and vehicle speed cross-check. Causes are a damaged reluctor wheel, debris at the sensor tip, a corroded connector, or chafed internal transmission wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0741 (Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance/Stuck Off) sets when the TCM detects an open circuit, out-of-range current, or a stuck-on/stuck-off performance fault while driving the torque converter clutch solenoid that locks the converter for fuel economy at cruise. Causes are a failed TCC solenoid, contaminated fluid causing the solenoid or clutch plate to stick, or damaged control wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Electrical
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0743 (Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Electrical) sets when the TCM detects an open circuit, out-of-range current, or a stuck-on/stuck-off performance fault while driving the torque converter clutch solenoid that locks the converter for fuel economy at cruise. Causes are a failed TCC solenoid, contaminated fluid causing the solenoid or clutch plate to stick, or damaged control wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Shift Solenoid B
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P0755 (Shift Solenoid B) sets when the TCM detects an open circuit, out-of-range current, or a stuck-on/stuck-off performance fault while driving one of the transmission's shift solenoids, which route hydraulic pressure to select the current gear. Every solenoid letter shares the same diagnosis path: causes are a failed solenoid coil, sludge/debris jamming the solenoid's spool, or damaged control wiring at the internal valve-body connector.

dtc_codes.title_en: OBD System Readiness Test Not Complete
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1000 (OBD System Readiness Test Not Complete) is a status indicator, not a fault: the powertrain module sets it after battery disconnection or code clearing until every OBD readiness monitor has completed its drive-cycle self-test. It clears itself once the drive cycle finishes; it stores no failure and triggers no repair by itself, but the vehicle will fail an emissions inspection while monitors remain incomplete.

dtc_codes.title_en: Fuel Control Mixture Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1083 (Fuel Control Mixture Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1) sets when the ECM must add more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a lean condition on the indicated bank. The leading causes are a vacuum or intake air leak downstream of the MAF, a weak fuel pump or clogged filter, or a leaking exhaust manifold gasket confusing the upstream O2 sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: Fuel Control Mixture Rich Bank 2 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1086 (Fuel Control Mixture Rich Bank 2 Sensor 1) sets when the ECM must remove more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a rich condition on the indicated bank. Leading causes are a leaking fuel injector, a stuck-open fuel pressure regulator, a fouled MAF sensor overreporting airflow, or a failing fuel pressure sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: BARO Sensor Circuit
dtc_codes.description_en: P1100 (BARO Sensor Circuit) points to the barometric pressure sensor (position A, B, or C on engines carrying more than one), whose ambient-pressure reading the ECM uses to correct fueling and boost targets for altitude. Many BARO sensors live inside the ECM itself, in which case the module is replaced rather than a discrete part; where the sensor is external, a blocked or contaminated sampling port, a corroded connector, and a drifted sensing element are the common causes of a signal that is out of range or frozen at one value.

dtc_codes.title_en: Long Term Fuel Trim Bank 1 System Too Lean
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1128 (Long Term Fuel Trim Bank 1 System Too Lean) sets when overall short- or long-term fuel trim for a bank moves outside its normal operating window without a specific lean or rich bias being isolated. Causes span vacuum leaks, a fuel delivery imbalance, or a fuel/air metering sensor reading incorrectly for that bank.

dtc_codes.title_en: Lack of Upstream Heated Oxygen Sensor Switch Sensor Indicates Lean Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1131 (Lack of Upstream Heated Oxygen Sensor Switch Sensor Indicates Lean Bank 1) sets when an oxygen sensor takes longer than the calibrated time to transition between rich and lean voltage states. This is typically a sensor element that has aged or been contaminated by silicone, oil ash, or coolant, though an exhaust leak that dilutes the sample can also slow the switching response.

dtc_codes.title_en: Air/Fuel Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1155 (Air/Fuel Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-spec resistance in the internal heater element of an oxygen sensor, or the heater fails to bring the sensor to operating temperature within the expected time. This is almost always a degraded heater element inside the O2 sensor itself, though a blown fuse, relay, or chafed heater wiring can also be responsible.

dtc_codes.title_en: VTEC System Malfunction Rear Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1259 (VTEC System Malfunction Rear Bank 1) sets when the ECM does not see the VTEC oil pressure switch confirm a cam-profile shift after commanding the VTEC spool valve solenoid, or detects an open/shorted condition on either component's circuit. VTEC (Variable valve Timing and lift Electronic Control) uses oil pressure routed through the spool valve to lock a pin between rocker arms for the high-lift cam lobe; the pressure switch confirms that pressure actually built before the ECM trusts the engagement. Low or degraded engine oil that cannot build switching pressure, a clogged VTEC oil strainer screen starving the spool valve, a failed pressure switch, or a spool valve solenoid with a sticking or shorted coil are the common causes.

dtc_codes.title_en: Ignition Signal
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1320 (Ignition Signal) sets when the ECM (or, on coil-on-plug systems with many cylinders, a dedicated ignition driver) detects an open circuit or out-of-range voltage while commanding a specific coil's primary winding, covering both the classic per-letter Ignition Coil Primary Control Circuit/Open codes and the newer Ignition [Letter] Control Signal Circuit Open/Low/High variants used on high-cylinder-count and coil-per-plug platforms. In every variant the physical fault sits in the same place: a failed coil primary winding, a corroded or unseated coil connector, or chafed wiring between the ECM/driver and that specific coil.

dtc_codes.title_en: CKP/CMP Correlation
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1345 (CKP/CMP Correlation) sets when the ECM compares crankshaft and camshaft position signals and finds their relative timing outside the expected window, or cannot establish a stable engine position sync. This is most often caused by timing chain/belt stretch or a jumped tooth, a failing crankshaft or camshaft position sensor, worn tensioner/guides, or reluctor-wheel damage.

dtc_codes.title_en: IC Circuit High Voltage
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1351 (IC Circuit High Voltage) sets when the ECM (or, on coil-on-plug systems with many cylinders, a dedicated ignition driver) detects an open circuit or out-of-range voltage while commanding a specific coil's primary winding, covering both the classic per-letter Ignition Coil Primary Control Circuit/Open codes and the newer Ignition [Letter] Control Signal Circuit Open/Low/High variants used on high-cylinder-count and coil-per-plug platforms. In every variant the physical fault sits in the same place: a failed coil primary winding, a corroded or unseated coil connector, or chafed wiring between the ECM/driver and that specific coil.

dtc_codes.title_en: Theft Deterrent Fuel Enable Signal Lost
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P1626 (Theft Deterrent Fuel Enable Signal Lost) sets when GM's theft-deterrent system fails to validate the key or drops the fuel-enable signal after a valid start, but the hardware behind that failure differs by generation: VATS/PASS-Key (roughly 1986-1996) reads a resistor pellet embedded in the key blade through contacts inside the ignition lock cylinder, while Passlock/PASS-Key III (roughly 1996 onward, the larger share of affected vehicles) uses a Hall-effect or inductive sensor in the lock cylinder that reads an ordinary or transponder key with no pellet at all. Because both generations share the same fault codes, the first diagnostic step is identifying which system the vehicle has from its model year and RPO code before choosing a repair path. Causes range from a worn or incorrect-resistance key pellet and corroded decoder-ring contacts on VATS vehicles to a failed lock-cylinder sensor or a chafed wire to the BCM on Passlock vehicles.

dtc_codes.title_en: No CCD Messages Received From PCM
dtc_codes.description_en: P1698 sets when the gateway or another control module stops receiving any messages from a powertrain-side module or smart sensor -- the ECM/PCM, TCM, or one of the engine-bay LIN-networked sensors (MAP, MAF, EGR, turbo boost, fuel pressure, and similar) that report over a low-speed sub-bus feeding into the high-speed backbone. These nodes live in the engine compartment where connectors see more heat-cycling, vibration, and oil/coolant contamination than any other module class, so a burned or corroded engine-harness connector is the leading cause, followed by a blown fuse for that module's dedicated power circuit.

dtc_codes.title_en: Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: P2002 (Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1) sets when the differential-pressure or soot-model calculation shows the diesel particulate filter is passing more particulate matter than its efficiency threshold allows, or when an abnormal pressure-drop signature indicates a cracked or missing filter substrate. A substrate cracked or melted by an uncontrolled regeneration event, a swapped-in filter that lacks the correct catalytic coating, and a leaking or misrouted differential-pressure sensor hose are the most common causes.

dtc_codes.title_en: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2096 (Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean Bank 1) sets when the ECM must add more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a lean condition on the indicated bank. The leading causes are a vacuum or intake air leak downstream of the MAF, a weak fuel pump or clogged filter, or a leaking exhaust manifold gasket confusing the upstream O2 sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2097 (Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich Bank 1) sets when the ECM must remove more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a rich condition on the indicated bank. Leading causes are a leaking fuel injector, a stuck-open fuel pressure regulator, a fouled MAF sensor overreporting airflow, or a failing fuel pressure sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: Throttle Actuator A Control Motor Circuit Range/Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: P2101 (Throttle Actuator A Control Motor Circuit Range/Performance) is set when the drive-by-wire throttle actuator motor's control circuit reports an open winding, a short, an out-of-range current draw, or the throttle plate's measured position that does not track the commanded motor current. Carbon and oil-vapor buildup on the throttle bore increasing motor load, a worn brush-type motor drawing excess current, and a corroded connector at the throttle body are the leading physical causes.

dtc_codes.title_en: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A/B Voltage Correlation
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2135 (Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A/B Voltage Correlation) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-range voltage, or an implausible rate of change, from a throttle body or accelerator pedal position sensor channel. Causes are a worn sensor track, a corroded connector, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch D/E Voltage Correlation
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2138 (Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch D/E Voltage Correlation) sets when the ECM detects an open, shorted, or out-of-range voltage, or an implausible rate of change, from a throttle body or accelerator pedal position sensor channel. Causes are a worn sensor track, a corroded connector, or chafed wiring between the sensor and the ECM.

dtc_codes.title_en: Cooling System Performance
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2181 (Cooling System Performance) sets when engine coolant fails to reach or maintain its regulating temperature within the expected time, or coolant flow/circulation is judged insufficient. Causes are a thermostat stuck open, a low coolant level, a failing water pump, or a chronically cold operating condition combined with a stuck-open thermostat.

dtc_codes.title_en: System Too Lean at Idle Bank 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2187 (System Too Lean at Idle Bank 1) sets when the ECM must add more fuel than the calibrated limit allows to correct a lean condition on the indicated bank. The leading causes are a vacuum or intake air leak downstream of the MAF, a weak fuel pump or clogged filter, or a leaking exhaust manifold gasket confusing the upstream O2 sensor.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2195 (O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, a stuck/biased voltage, or no signal activity from an oxygen sensor's signal circuit. Causes are a contaminated or worn-out sensor element, an exhaust leak near the sensor bung skewing readings, or damaged sensor wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P2270 (O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 2) sets when the ECM sees an open circuit, a stuck/biased voltage, or no signal activity from an oxygen sensor's signal circuit. Causes are a contaminated or worn-out sensor element, an exhaust leak near the sensor bung skewing readings, or damaged sensor wiring.

dtc_codes.title_en: Fuel level is too low, High voltage battery assembly failure, High voltage battery is not sufficiently charged
dtc_codes.description_en: Code P3000 (Fuel level is too low, High voltage battery assembly failure, High voltage battery is not sufficiently charged) sets when the overall HV bus voltage - measured system-wide rather than at any single battery pack or contactor - reads outside its expected window or fails an ECM performance check. Because this is a system-level measurement, causes span a genuinely low/high pack state of charge, a contactor not fully seating, or a fault in the HV bus voltage-sense circuit itself rather than any single named component.

dtc_codes.title_en: Lost Communication With ECM/PCM A
dtc_codes.description_en: U0100 sets when the gateway or another control module stops receiving any messages from a powertrain-side module or smart sensor -- the ECM/PCM, TCM, or one of the engine-bay LIN-networked sensors (MAP, MAF, EGR, turbo boost, fuel pressure, and similar) that report over a low-speed sub-bus feeding into the high-speed backbone. These nodes live in the engine compartment where connectors see more heat-cycling, vibration, and oil/coolant contamination than any other module class, so a burned or corroded engine-harness connector is the leading cause, followed by a blown fuse for that module's dedicated power circuit.

dtc_codes.title_en: Lost Communication With TCM
dtc_codes.description_en: U0101 sets when the gateway or another control module stops receiving any messages from a powertrain-side module or smart sensor -- the ECM/PCM, TCM, or one of the engine-bay LIN-networked sensors (MAP, MAF, EGR, turbo boost, fuel pressure, and similar) that report over a low-speed sub-bus feeding into the high-speed backbone. These nodes live in the engine compartment where connectors see more heat-cycling, vibration, and oil/coolant contamination than any other module class, so a burned or corroded engine-harness connector is the leading cause, followed by a blown fuse for that module's dedicated power circuit.

dtc_codes.title_en: Lost Communication With Anti-Lock Brake System (ABS) Control Module A
dtc_codes.description_en: U0121 indicates loss of contact with a chassis-dynamics module -- ABS/stability control, steering angle sensor, ride-height/suspension control, power steering, or a differential/brake-blending actuator -- all mounted low near the subframe, wheel wells, or under-floor tunnel where connectors take the worst exposure to road salt, water spray, and vibration of any module class. Unlike cabin electronics, these connectors are often sealed but still fail at the seal itself after years of thermal cycling, so a corroded or water-intruded low-mount connector is the dominant cause ahead of any harness break.

repair_fixes.title: Inspect wheel speed sensor connector and harness routing
repair_fixes.steps: Locate the sensor connector near the hub or knuckle at the affected corner • Unplug and inspect for corrosion, moisture, or a bent pin • Follow the harness up to the body grommet checking for chafing against the strut or subframe • Clean, reseat, clear the code, and road test

repair_fixes.title: Test wheel speed sensor resistance and signal
repair_fixes.steps: Unplug the sensor and measure coil resistance against the factory specification • Reconnect and back-probe the signal circuit while rotating the wheel by hand • Confirm a clean, consistent AC signal with no dropouts • Replace the sensor if resistance is out of range or the signal is erratic

repair_fixes.title: Replace wheel speed sensor
repair_fixes.steps: Disconnect the battery negative terminal • Remove the sensor mounting bolt and pull the sensor from the knuckle • Install the replacement sensor, confirming it seats fully against the tone ring • Clear the code and confirm signal quality across a range of speeds

repair_fixes.title: Repair chafed wheel speed sensor harness wiring
repair_fixes.steps: Trace the harness from the sensor to the body connector along the strut and control arm • Identify the chafe point, commonly where the harness crosses suspension travel • Repair damaged conductors with solder and heat-shrink, then re-route and secure the harness • Clear codes and confirm all four corners correlate correctly on a road test

repair_fixes.title: Adjust brake pedal switch plunger clearance
repair_fixes.steps: Locate the brake pedal switch mounted on the pedal bracket above the pedal arm • Loosen the switch locknut and adjust plunger contact per the service manual clearance spec • Pull the pedal fully rearward to auto-adjust the switch on platforms that support it • Verify stop lamps and scan tool brake switch PID respond correctly to pedal travel

repair_fixes.title: Inspect brake pedal switch connector
repair_fixes.steps: Unplug the switch connector and inspect pins for corrosion • Clean with electrical contact cleaner and reseat the connector • Confirm both switch channels toggle together with a multimeter • Clear the code and verify stop lamp operation

repair_fixes.title: Replace brake pedal switch
repair_fixes.steps: Disconnect the battery negative terminal • Rotate and remove the switch from the pedal bracket • Install the replacement switch and adjust plunger clearance to spec • Clear codes and confirm correct stop lamp and brake-applied signal operation

repair_fixes.title: Repair stop lamp/brake switch circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: Trace the harness from the switch to the module and stop lamp fuse • Check for chafing near the pedal bracket and steering column • Repair with solder and heat-shrink where damaged • Verify both switch channels and stop lamps function correctly

repair_fixes.title: Change engine oil and filter to spec viscosity
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Drain and inspect oil condition for sludge or debris • 2. Replace with OEM-viscosity oil and a new filter • 3. Clear codes and run a phaser sweep test with a scan tool • 4. Road test through varied load to confirm stable timing

repair_fixes.title: Replace oil control valve and clean phaser feed passage
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the OCV solenoid and inspect its filter screen • 2. Clean the oil feed passage to the phaser of sludge with solvent and compressed air • 3. Install a new OCV solenoid • 4. Clear adaptive learning and verify timing response

repair_fixes.title: Replace worn camshaft phaser assembly
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Set the engine to TDC and lock the timing chain • 2. Remove the worn phaser and inspect the chain/tensioner for related wear • 3. Install the new phaser and retime to factory marks • 4. Verify actuator sweep and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Correct timing chain/belt installation
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the timing cover and verify marks against factory specification • 2. Correct any tooth-count misalignment on the chain or belt • 3. Replace the tensioner and guides while accessed • 4. Confirm cam/crank correlation and phaser response

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and replace crankshaft/camshaft position sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Identify which sensor the correlation fault points to on the scan tool freeze frame • 2. Unplug and remove the affected position sensor • 3. Inspect the reluctor wheel/tone ring for chips or debris • 4. Install the new sensor with correct air-gap shim and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Inspect timing chain/belt for stretch or jumped timing
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the timing cover and verify cam-to-crank alignment against factory timing marks • 2. Measure chain stretch or check belt tooth wear • 3. Replace the timing chain/belt, tensioner, and guides as a set • 4. Reset timing to factory marks and verify correlation with a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Repair crank/cam sensor wiring and connectors
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the sensor signal and ground at each connector while cranking • 2. Voltage-drop test the harness runs back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed conductors near the timing cover with heat-shrink splices • 4. Confirm clean square-wave signals on a scope

repair_fixes.title: Inspect intake ducting and clamps downstream of the MAF
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Inspect the intake duct between the MAF and the throttle body for cracks or splits • 2. Check every clamp downstream of the sensor for looseness

repair_fixes.title: Clean MAF sensing element
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the intake duct clamp and unplug the MAF connector • 2. Remove the sensor with a security Torx bit • 3. Spray the hot-wire element with dedicated MAF cleaner (never touch it) • 4. Reinstall, clear the code, and road test

repair_fixes.title: Smoke-test the intake tract downstream of the MAF for leaks
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Smoke-test or spray-test the intake tract between the MAF and throttle body

repair_fixes.title: Replace cracked intake boots and couplers downstream of the MAF
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Replace cracked intake boots and hardened couplers • 2. Torque all clamps and verify fuel trims return toward 0% at idle

repair_fixes.title: Test MAF 5V reference, signal and ground circuits
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the 5V reference, signal, and ground at the MAF connector • 2. Perform a voltage-drop test on each leg back to the ECM • 3. Confirm live airflow (g/s) tracks RPM on a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Repair MAF circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Repair chafed or corroded conductors found in the circuit test with solder and heat-shrink • 2. Confirm live airflow (g/s) tracks RPM on a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Replace mass air flow sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal • 2. Unplug the MAF harness connector and remove the sensor screws • 3. Install the replacement sensor without touching the element • 4. Reconnect and perform an ECU idle relearn if the platform requires it

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean MAP sensor vacuum port
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the MAP sensor on the intake manifold • 2. Remove and inspect the vacuum port for oil or debris • 3. Clean the port and sensor housing • 4. Reinstall and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Replace MAP/barometric pressure sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Unplug the sensor connector • 2. Remove the sensor from the manifold or its remote mount • 3. Install the replacement sensor with a new O-ring • 4. Clear codes and verify reading against known altitude/barometric baseline

repair_fixes.title: Repair MAP sensor circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the 5V reference, signal, and ground at the connector • 2. Voltage-drop test each leg back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded conductors with heat-shrink splices • 4. Confirm signal tracks vacuum/boost changes smoothly

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean IAT sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the IAT sensor in the intake tube or integrated into the MAF housing • 2. Unplug and inspect for corrosion or debris • 3. Clean contacts and apply dielectric grease • 4. Reconnect and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Replace intake air temperature sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the affected IAT sensor per the bank/position in the code • 2. Disconnect and remove the sensor from its bore • 3. Install the replacement sensor with a new seal • 4. Clear codes and verify reading tracks ambient at cold start

repair_fixes.title: Repair IAT sensor circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Measure sensor resistance at the connector against a temperature/resistance chart • 2. Voltage-drop test the circuit back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded wiring near the intake tract with heat-shrink splices • 4. Confirm stable readings across temperature swings

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean IAT sensor connector

repair_fixes.title: Top off coolant and inspect ECT sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Check coolant level and top off with the correct spec coolant • 2. Unplug the ECT sensor connector and inspect for corrosion • 3. Clean contacts and reconnect • 4. Clear codes and monitor warm-up temperature curve

repair_fixes.title: Replace engine/radiator coolant temperature sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Relieve cooling system pressure and drain coolant to below sensor level • 2. Remove the sensor from the head, housing, or radiator tank • 3. Install the replacement sensor with sealant or new seal as specified • 4. Refill coolant, bleed air, and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Repair coolant temperature sensor wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Measure sensor resistance at the connector against a temperature/resistance chart • 2. Voltage-drop test the circuit back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded wiring with heat-shrink splices • 4. Confirm reading tracks actual coolant temperature

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean throttle/pedal position sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the throttle body or accelerator pedal assembly connector • 2. Unplug and inspect for corrosion or bent pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat firmly • 4. Clear codes and verify smooth voltage sweep

repair_fixes.title: Replace throttle body or pedal position sensor assembly
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Unplug the connector and remove the mounting fasteners • 2. Install the replacement throttle body or pedal assembly • 3. Reconnect and perform a throttle relearn if required • 4. Clear codes and verify all channels track together

repair_fixes.title: Repair throttle/pedal position sensor wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the reference, signal, and ground circuits at the connector • 2. Voltage-drop test each leg back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed conductors with heat-shrink splices • 4. Confirm all sensor channels agree throughout the pedal/throttle sweep

repair_fixes.title: Check coolant level and inspect for external leaks
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Check coolant level cold and top off to spec • 2. Inspect hoses, radiator, and water pump weep hole for leaks • 3. Repair any obvious external leak source • 4. Clear codes and monitor warm-up time

repair_fixes.title: Replace stuck-open thermostat
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Drain coolant below the thermostat housing • 2. Remove the housing and replace the thermostat and gasket • 3. Refill coolant and bleed air from the system • 4. Confirm engine reaches operating temperature within expected time

repair_fixes.title: Replace failing water pump
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Drain coolant and remove drive components to access the water pump • 2. Remove the worn pump and inspect the impeller and bearing • 3. Install the replacement pump with a new gasket • 4. Refill, bleed, and verify stable circulation and temperature

repair_fixes.title: Inspect for exhaust leaks near the O2 sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Inspect the exhaust manifold and pipe joints near the sensor bung for leaks • 2. Listen and smoke-test for exhaust leaks upstream of the sensor • 3. Replace gaskets or tighten fasteners as needed • 4. Clear codes and monitor sensor voltage trace

repair_fixes.title: Replace oxygen sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Identify the affected bank/sensor position • 2. Remove the sensor with an O2 sensor socket • 3. Apply anti-seize to threads (avoid the tip) and install the new sensor • 4. Clear codes and confirm a normal switching voltage trace

repair_fixes.title: Repair O2 sensor signal circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the signal and ground at the connector with the engine running • 2. Voltage-drop test the circuit back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded wiring near the exhaust with high-temp splices • 4. Confirm proper switching activity

repair_fixes.title: Inspect for contamination sources (oil, coolant, silicone) reaching the exhaust
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Check for oil consumption, coolant leaks, or recent use of silicone sealant near the intake/exhaust • 2. Repair the contamination source if found • 3. Inspect the sensor tip for a sooty or white/gray glassy coating • 4. Clear codes after addressing the source

repair_fixes.title: Replace slow-responding oxygen sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Identify the affected bank/sensor position • 2. Remove with an O2 sensor socket and inspect the old sensor tip for contamination • 3. Apply anti-seize and install the new sensor • 4. Clear codes and verify switching frequency improves

repair_fixes.title: Repair exhaust leak diluting sensor sample
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Smoke-test the exhaust system upstream of the affected sensor • 2. Replace leaking gaskets or cracked pipe sections • 3. Torque fasteners to spec • 4. Clear codes and re-verify switching speed

repair_fixes.title: Test O2 sensor heater circuit fuse and relay
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the O2 heater fuse and relay in the underhood fuse box • 2. Inspect and test with a multimeter for continuity and proper switching • 3. Replace any blown fuse or failed relay • 4. Clear codes and verify heater current draw

repair_fixes.title: Replace oxygen sensor with failed heater
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Identify the affected bank/sensor position from the code • 2. Unplug the connector and remove the sensor with an O2 sensor socket • 3. Apply anti-seize to threads (avoid the sensor tip) and install the new sensor • 4. Reconnect and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Repair O2 heater circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Measure heater element resistance at the connector against spec • 2. Voltage-drop test the heater supply and ground legs • 3. Repair chafed or corroded wiring near the exhaust manifold with high-temp splices • 4. Confirm heater current draw matches spec

repair_fixes.title: Inspect for exhaust leaks near the O2 sensor

repair_fixes.title: Test O2 sensor heater circuit fuse and relay
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the O2 heater fuse and relay in the underhood fuse box • 2. Inspect and test with a multimeter for continuity and proper switching • 3. Replace any blown fuse or failed relay • 4. Clear codes and verify heater current draw

repair_fixes.title: Replace oxygen sensor with failed heater
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Identify the affected bank/sensor position from the code • 2. Unplug the connector and remove the sensor with an O2 sensor socket • 3. Apply anti-seize to threads (avoid the sensor tip) and install the new sensor • 4. Reconnect and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Repair O2 heater circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Measure heater element resistance at the connector against spec • 2. Voltage-drop test the heater supply and ground legs • 3. Repair chafed or corroded wiring near the exhaust manifold with high-temp splices • 4. Confirm heater current draw matches spec

repair_fixes.title: Smoke-test intake for vacuum/air leaks
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Connect a smoke machine to the intake at idle • 2. Watch for smoke escaping at intake gaskets, PCV hoses, or brake booster line • 3. Replace any leaking gasket or hose • 4. Clear codes and verify fuel trims return toward 0%

repair_fixes.title: Replace fuel filter and test fuel pump output
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Replace the fuel filter if serviceable • 2. Measure fuel pump pressure and volume against spec under load • 3. Replace a weak pump if it fails the test • 4. Clear codes and confirm rail pressure holds steady

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and repair exhaust manifold gasket leak
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Inspect the exhaust manifold gasket and studs near the upstream O2 sensor for leaks • 2. Replace the gasket and any corroded studs • 3. Torque to spec in sequence • 4. Clear codes and re-verify trim correction

repair_fixes.title: Clean MAF sensor and inspect for false-high airflow readings
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the MAF sensor and inspect the hot-wire element for contamination • 2. Clean with dedicated MAF cleaner (never touch the element) • 3. Reinstall and clear codes • 4. Compare live MAF g/s reading against expected values

repair_fixes.title: Test fuel injectors for leakage and replace as needed
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Perform a fuel injector leak-down/drip test • 2. Identify any injector leaking past its seat • 3. Replace the faulty injector(s) and seals • 4. Clear codes and verify trims return toward 0%

repair_fixes.title: Replace stuck-open fuel pressure regulator
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Depressurize the fuel system • 2. Remove the regulator and inspect the diaphragm/valve for sticking • 3. Install the replacement regulator with new seals • 4. Clear codes and confirm rail pressure holds at commanded target

repair_fixes.title: Replace spark plugs and inspect ignition coils as a set
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Retrieve freeze-frame data to see which cylinders were flagged • 2. Remove and inspect all spark plugs for wear, fouling, or incorrect gap • 3. Replace the full set with OE-spec plugs • 4. Swap coils between cylinders if a weak coil is suspected • 5. Clear codes and monitor misfire counters on a drive cycle

repair_fixes.title: Smoke-test intake and vacuum lines for a shared leak
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Connect a smoke machine at the intake tract with all accessory vacuum ports capped • 2. Watch for smoke escaping at intake gaskets, PCV hoses, or brake booster lines • 3. Replace any cracked hose or gasket found • 4. Clear the code and verify fuel trims return to normal

repair_fixes.title: Verify fuel delivery and refuel if the tank is low
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Check the fuel gauge and refuel above one-quarter tank if low • 2. Scan for low fuel pressure or pump duty-cycle codes stored alongside the misfire • 3. Clear the code and complete a drive cycle to confirm it does not return

repair_fixes.title: Test fuel pump output pressure and delivery volume
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Connect a fuel pressure gauge to the test port or rail • 2. Compare static and key-on pressure to spec • 3. Perform a timed volume test at the return line if accessible • 4. Replace a fuel pump that cannot hold pressure or deliver volume under load

repair_fixes.title: Swap spark plug and ignition coil to confirm the cylinder
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the coil and plug from the misfiring cylinder • 2. Inspect the plug for fouling, wear, or an incorrect gap • 3. Swap the coil with a known-good adjacent cylinder's coil • 4. Clear the code and see if the misfire follows the coil or stays with the cylinder • 5. Replace the plug and/or coil based on the result

repair_fixes.title: Test and clean or replace the cylinder's fuel injector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Perform an injector balance or ohms test on the affected cylinder • 2. Swap the injector with a neighboring cylinder to see if the misfire follows • 3. Clean the injector on an ultrasonic bench or replace it • 4. Reinstall with new O-rings and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Run a cylinder compression or leak-down test
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Disable fuel and ignition for a dry compression test on all cylinders • 2. Compare the flagged cylinder's reading against its neighbors • 3. Add oil and retest (wet test) to isolate rings vs. valves • 4. Follow up with a leak-down test to confirm the exact leak path

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and replace a leaking or damaged cylinder head gasket/valve
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm the leak-down result points to a head gasket or valve seat • 2. Remove the valve cover/head as required for access • 3. Replace the head gasket or recondition the valve seat • 4. Reassemble to torque spec and verify compression returns to spec

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and reseat the knock sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the knock sensor(s), usually threaded into the block under the intake manifold • 2. Unplug and inspect for oil contamination or corroded pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat the connector • 4. Clear the code and monitor knock counts on a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Replace the knock sensor at correct torque spec
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the intake manifold or components blocking sensor access • 2. Unbolt the failed knock sensor • 3. Install the replacement and torque to the exact factory spec (over- or under-torquing causes false readings) • 4. Reconnect, clear codes, and verify signal activity while revving the engine

repair_fixes.title: Repair knock sensor circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the signal and shield/ground legs at the sensor connector • 2. Voltage-drop test the harness back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded conductors with soldered, heat-shrunk, shielded splices • 4. Confirm a clean knock signal waveform on a scope

repair_fixes.title: Diagnose knock control module/ECM internal fault
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm all sensors and wiring test good in isolation • 2. Check for a shared power/ground fault affecting the knock control circuit • 3. Update or reflash ECM software if a known knock-strategy bulletin applies • 4. Replace the ECM only after all external causes are ruled out

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and reseat the crankshaft position sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the sensor near the crank pulley or bellhousing • 2. Unplug and inspect for oil intrusion or corroded pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat until it clicks • 4. Clear the code and crank the engine to verify a start

repair_fixes.title: Replace the crankshaft position sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the sensor's retaining bolt and withdraw it from its bore • 2. Inspect the reluctor wheel/tone ring for damaged teeth or debris • 3. Install the replacement sensor, setting the air gap per spec if not self-adjusting • 4. Clear codes and confirm a stable RPM signal at idle and under load

repair_fixes.title: Repair crankshaft position sensor circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the signal, shield, and ground legs at the sensor connector • 2. Voltage-drop test each leg back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded conductors with soldered, heat-shrunk splices • 4. Confirm a clean signal waveform on a scope while cranking

repair_fixes.title: Clean or replace a damaged reluctor wheel/tone ring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the sensor and inspect the reluctor wheel through the access bore or with the crank pulley/cover removed • 2. Clean off accumulated debris or rust • 3. Replace a reluctor wheel with bent, missing, or chipped teeth • 4. Reinstall the sensor, reset the gap, and verify a clean signal

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and reseat the camshaft position sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the sensor at the valve cover, timing cover, or distributor housing per platform • 2. Unplug and inspect for oil intrusion or corroded pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat fully • 4. Clear the code and verify the engine restarts promptly

repair_fixes.title: Replace the camshaft position sensor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the sensor's retaining bolt and withdraw it from its bore • 2. Inspect the O-ring and trigger wheel for wear or debris • 3. Install the replacement sensor with a fresh O-ring • 4. Clear codes and confirm cylinder identification on a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Repair camshaft position sensor circuit wiring
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Back-probe the signal, reference, and ground legs at the sensor connector • 2. Voltage-drop test each leg back to the ECM • 3. Repair chafed or corroded conductors with soldered, heat-shrunk splices • 4. Confirm a clean signal waveform on a scope while cranking

repair_fixes.title: Inspect the camshaft trigger wheel for timing-related damage
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove valve cover components as needed to view the trigger wheel • 2. Check for chipped, bent, or slipped trigger wheel teeth from a prior timing chain/belt issue • 3. Correct the underlying timing fault and replace a damaged trigger wheel • 4. Reinstall the sensor and verify cam-crank correlation with a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and reseat the camshaft position sensor connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the sensor at the valve cover, timing cover, or distributor housing per platform • 2. Unplug and inspect for oil intrusion or corroded pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat fully • 4. Clear the code and verify the engine restarts promptly

repair_fixes.title: Replace the camshaft position sensor

repair_fixes.title: Inspect the camshaft trigger wheel for timing-related damage
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove valve cover components as needed to view the trigger wheel • 2. Check for chipped, bent, or slipped trigger wheel teeth from a prior timing chain/belt issue • 3. Correct the underlying timing fault and replace a damaged trigger wheel • 4. Reinstall the sensor and verify cam-crank correlation with a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Clean the EGR valve and passages of carbon buildup
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the EGR valve from the intake manifold • 2. Scrape and solvent-clean carbon deposits from the valve pintle and seat • 3. Clean or snake out the connecting EGR passages/tube • 4. Reinstall with a new gasket and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean the EGR cooler for restriction
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate and remove the EGR cooler from the exhaust/coolant circuit • 2. Inspect for soot buildup restricting the internal passages • 3. Clean with an approved solvent or replace if clogged/cracked internally • 4. Reinstall with new gaskets/clamps and clear codes

repair_fixes.title: Test EGR valve position sensor tracking and valve travel
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the EGR valve through its full range with a scan tool • 2. Monitor commanded vs. actual position sensor feedback • 3. Replace the valve if it does not reach commanded positions or the sensor does not track smoothly • 4. Clear the code and verify flow response

repair_fixes.title: Replace a mechanically stuck or worn EGR valve
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm cleaning did not restore free valve movement • 2. Remove and replace the EGR valve assembly • 3. Install with a new gasket and torque to spec • 4. Clear codes and verify commanded flow is achieved

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and clean the EGR cooler for restriction

repair_fixes.title: Test EGR valve position sensor tracking and valve travel
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the EGR valve through its full range with a scan tool • 2. Monitor commanded vs. actual position sensor feedback • 3. Replace the valve if it does not reach commanded positions or the sensor does not track smoothly • 4. Clear the code and verify flow response

repair_fixes.title: Replace a mechanically stuck or worn EGR valve
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm cleaning did not restore free valve movement • 2. Remove and replace the EGR valve assembly • 3. Install with a new gasket and torque to spec • 4. Clear codes and verify commanded flow is achieved

repair_fixes.title: Inspect and reseat the EGR valve/throttle connector
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the EGR valve or EGR throttle connector • 2. Unplug and inspect for carbon contamination or corroded pins • 3. Clean contacts and reseat fully • 4. Clear the code and command the valve with a scan tool

repair_fixes.title: Free a carbon-stuck EGR valve/throttle and clean the bore
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the valve or throttle body from its mounting • 2. Scrape and solvent-clean carbon from the pintle/plate and bore • 3. Verify smooth full-range movement by hand before reinstalling • 4. Reinstall with a new gasket, clear codes, and command through full range

repair_fixes.title: Replace the EGR control valve/throttle solenoid or motor
repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm cleaning did not restore proper electrical/mechanical response • 2. Remove and replace the valve/throttle assembly • 3. Install with a new gasket, torqued to spec • 4. Clear codes and verify commanded vs. actual position match

repair_fixes.title: Repair EGR control circuit wiring back to the ECM

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the switching valve with a scan tool while listening/feeling for valve movement • 2. Inspect the valve and its connector for carbon or corrosion • 3. Replace a valve that does not switch cleanly • 4. Clear codes and verify flow direction changes correctly

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the AIR pump on with a scan tool and listen/feel for operation • 2. Check the pump relay and fuse if it does not run • 3. Replace a pump that is seized, noisy, or produces insufficient flow • 4. Clear codes and verify flow readings meet spec

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Trace the purge line from the canister to the intake/throttle body • 2. Look for a kinked, collapsed, or pinched section, especially near heat sources • 3. Replace the damaged hose section • 4. Clear the code and monitor purge flow on a scan tool

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the purge solenoid with a scan tool while monitoring flow/vacuum • 2. Bench-test the solenoid for proper sealing when de-energized and full flow when energized • 3. Replace a solenoid that leaks or restricts flow • 4. Clear codes and verify purge flow matches command

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Remove the canister and inspect for saturated or degraded carbon media restricting flow • 2. Replace the canister if internally restricted • 3. Reinstall with new seals • 4. Clear the code and verify purge flow normalizes

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Compare the purge flow sensor's reading against a known commanded duty cycle • 2. Inspect the sensor's connector and mounting for damage • 3. Replace the sensor if it reads inconsistently with actual system behavior • 4. Clear codes and verify flow data now tracks correctly

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the vent solenoid, typically near the charcoal canister under the vehicle • 2. Unplug and inspect for corrosion, mud, or road-spray damage • 3. Clean contacts and reseat fully • 4. Clear the code and command the valve with a scan tool

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Disconnect the vent solenoid's air inlet and electrical connector • 2. Verify sealing and switching function with a hand pump before condemning it • 3. Install the replacement solenoid • 4. Clear the code and re-run the EVAP monitor

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Locate the vent solenoid's fresh-air inlet filter/port • 2. Clear mud, leaves, or ice blocking the intake • 3. Verify free valve movement by hand or with a scan-tool command • 4. Clear the code and re-run the EVAP monitor

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Confirm the fuel cap is present, undamaged, and threaded on correctly • 2. Replace a cracked or missing cap • 3. Clear the code and complete an EVAP drive cycle

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Visually trace the EVAP hose routing from the tank to the canister and engine • 2. Look for a hose knocked loose, split, or chewed by rodents • 3. Reconnect or replace the damaged section • 4. Smoke-test to confirm the leak is closed

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Command the vent valve closed with a scan tool and verify it holds vacuum with a hand pump • 2. Replace a valve that will not seal • 3. Reinstall and clear codes • 4. Re-run the EVAP monitor to confirm the large-leak fault clears

repair_fixes.steps: 1. Apply controlled test pressure/vacuum to the fuel tank via the service port • 2. Monitor for a leak at the fuel sending unit seal or tank seam • 3. Replace the sending unit seal or repair the tank as needed • 4. Clear codes and confirm the system holds
